title: The baptism (Matthew 3:13–17)
hookLine: Jesus goes under the Jordan, and a voice says: this is my beloved son

lines: A MAN FROM NAZARETH JOINS THE LINE.
cards: Some words can't be earned. Nobody is called beloved because of a good report card. At the Jordan, John is baptizing crowds, people turning around and starting again.
One day a man from Nazareth, about thirty years old, joins the line. He hasn't preached a sermon. He hasn't healed anyone.
As far as anyone knows, he's a builder from a small town in Galilee. And John looks at him and stops.

teach.b: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo: to dip, to plunge, to immerse, an ordinary Greek word for putting something under. John tries to refuse: "I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?"
Jesus answers: "Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness." Suffer here means allow.

teach.h: HE STANDS IN LINE WITH EVERYONE.
teach.b: So he goes down into the water, like everyone else in the line. Readers have asked ever since why he would stand with people turning from their wrongs. One old answer: he chose to stand exactly where they stood.
He comes up out of the water, and "the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him."
And a voice from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Look at the timing. No miracles yet, no teaching, no followers.
Beloved first; the work comes after.

Christians who confess the Trinity see it here: the Father's voice, the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, in one scene. Catholics and others in the West keep a feast of the Baptism of the Lord.
Orthodox Christians call it Theophany, God shown, and bless water. Baptism became the door into the church, though churches do it differently.
Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans and Anglicans baptize babies. Baptists and others baptize those old enough to profess faith. Some pour, some sprinkle, some go all the way under.
The words said over the water come from the end of Matthew's Gospel: in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

how: Christians are baptized with water, usually in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit: as infants in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican churches, and as believers in Baptist and many other churches. Many churches keep the Baptism of the Lord in January, and Orthodox Christians bless water at Theophany.

o: a dipping in water, a door to new life
a promise to give up wrongs forever
a blessing with oil on a newborn's head

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: to dip, to plunge, to immerse

s: John was eager to baptize Jesus
he tried to refuse: I have need to be baptized of thee.
the voice calls him beloved before any miracle or sermon
in Matthew, this comes before his ministry begins.
all churches baptize the same way
some baptize infants, some believers; some pour, some sprinkle, some immerse.

games.q: you're John. the man you've been saying is mightier than you walks into the river and asks you to baptize him. what do you do?
o: baptize him quickly, like everyone else.
try to refuse: you should baptize me.
games.why: John tries to refuse. Jesus answers, suffer it to be so now, and John baptizes him.

practice: If you can, hold your hands under warm running water at a sink and feel it run slowly over your fingers and palms; if you can't get to water, rest your hands open in your lap and imagine it.
While it runs, notice that you haven't done anything to earn this moment; you're just here. If you pray, hear the word beloved as spoken to you; if not, let the water be water.

wordCard.voice: Baptism. From the Greek for dip or plunge. Washing with water as a door into a new life, and the scene where Jesus is called beloved before he does a thing.

orig.note: Greek: to dip, to plunge, to immerse. An ordinary word for dipping, before it became a church word.

carryVoice: Your line: beloved, before anything else. Tomorrow that word gets tested. See you in the desert.
